practice.stem: Polo's description of the city's crafts and merchants best supports which claim about Song China?

options.A: Its economy depended mostly on the labor of enslaved workers in its cities.
options.B: Its cities were centers of large-scale manufacturing and trade.
options.C: Its merchants were forbidden to sell goods to other cities.
options.D: Its craftsmen made goods mainly for the emperor and his officials at court.

practice.explanation: Polo describes guilds of craftsmen, very rich merchants, and busy markets. His numbers may be exaggerated, but his account shows that making and selling goods were central to Song city life.

whyNot.A: Polo describes guilds of workmen and very wealthy merchants, not enslaved workers.
whyNot.C: Polo says the city supplied "many other cities of the kingdom."
whyNot.D: The goods were sold widely to other cities and in huge markets, not made just for the emperor.

practice.hint: Look at what the guilds made and where their goods went.

practice.stem: Historians should be careful with the numbers in the second paragraph mainly because

options.A: Polo counted the houses himself and made mistakes in his arithmetic
options.B: Mongol officials kept no records of the city's population or trade
options.C: they come from a plea asking a conqueror to spare the city
options.D: the numbers describe Venice, which Polo was comparing to Hangzhou

practice.explanation: The figures came from a statement written to the Mongol general. Its goal was to make him spare the city. A writer with that goal had reason to make the city sound as grand as possible.

whyNot.A: Polo says the numbers came from "the document aforesaid," not from his own count.
whyNot.B: Polo does not say whether the Mongols kept records, and that is not why the numbers are doubtful.
whyNot.D: The numbers describe Kinsay (Hangzhou), not Venice.

practice.hint: Read the end of the first paragraph. Why was the document written?

practice.stem: Polo's description of Hangzhou is most similar to descriptions of which other city?

options.A: Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Mexica Empire
options.B: Cuzco, the capital of the Inca Empire
options.C: Great Zimbabwe, the capital of a southern African kingdom
options.D: Timbuktu, a trading city of the Mali Empire

practice.explanation: Like Hangzhou, Tenochtitlan used canals and boats to move goods to busy markets. Its giant market at Tlatelolco amazed Spanish visitors in 1519.

whyNot.B: Cuzco was a great capital, but it was a mountain city, not a city of canals and boats.
whyNot.C: Great Zimbabwe was a stone-walled inland capital, not a city of canals and boats.
whyNot.D: Timbuktu was a trade and learning center, but it was not built around canals.

practice.hint: Think about how people and goods moved around Hangzhou. Then test each city in the choices.

practice.stem: The memorial best illustrates which feature of Song government?

options.A: Military generals made most decisions and gave orders directly to the emperor.
options.B: Scholar-officials were expected to advise and correct the emperor.
options.C: Buddhist monks controlled the treasury and decided how silk was used.
options.D: Wealthy merchants bought government posts and set the empire's tax rates.

practice.explanation: Song emperors relied on scholar-officials. Many earned their posts by passing exams on Confucian texts. Censors were expected to report wrongdoing and criticize bad decisions, even the emperor's.

whyNot.A: The writer is a scholar-official serving as a censor, not a general.
whyNot.C: The memorial does not mention Buddhist monks; the Treasury and the emperor decide spending.
whyNot.D: Ouyang Xiu earned his post by passing the civil service exams, not by buying it.

practice.hint: What was Ouyang Xiu's job, and what did it require him to do?

practice.stem: Ouyang Xiu's main purpose in the memorial was to

options.A: ask the emperor to raise the pay of workers in the Dyeing Department
options.B: convince the emperor to send a trade mission to Southeast Asia
options.C: request that Lady Chang be named empress in place of the current empress
options.D: persuade the emperor to cut palace spending and favors to relatives

practice.explanation: Ouyang Xiu says the palace spends too much. He also says Lady Chang's family gets too many gifts. He asks the emperor to "rectify these abuses."

whyNot.A: He mentions the dyers' suffering to show the cost of waste, not to ask for higher pay.
whyNot.B: The memorial is about palace spending, not trade abroad.
whyNot.C: He warns against Lady Chang's relatives receiving too much; he does not ask to raise her rank.

practice.hint: Look at the last sentence. What does he want the emperor to do?

practice.stem: Ouyang Xiu's warning that the emperor's actions might bring "divine wrath" is best explained by the Chinese belief that

options.A: the emperor was a living god whose decisions could not be questioned
options.B: Buddhist monks could punish rulers who spent too much on their families
options.C: the emperor's officials were chosen by priests who spoke for the gods
options.D: an emperor could lose the Mandate of Heaven by ruling badly

practice.explanation: Chinese rulers claimed the Mandate of Heaven, or Heaven's approval to rule. People believed Heaven could take it away from a bad ruler. So a loyal official warned the emperor in time.

whyNot.A: If the emperor could not be questioned, a censor like Ouyang Xiu would not be warning him.
whyNot.B: The memorial appeals to Heaven's judgment. It does not give Buddhist monks any power to punish the emperor.
whyNot.C: Song officials were chosen mainly by civil service exams, not by priests.

practice.hint: Which Chinese idea connected Heaven's approval with good rule?

practice.stem: The scene in the painting best illustrates which feature of the Song economy?

options.A: A farming economy in which families grew food for themselves rather than for sale
options.B: A government ban on private trade outside the emperor's palace
options.C: A busy commercial life of shops, markets, and goods moving by water and road
options.D: A shortage of workers that left Song cities nearly empty

practice.explanation: The scroll shows shops, restaurants, vendors, porters, carts, and boats. Song China's economy was very commercial. People bought and sold goods for money.

whyNot.A: The painting shows a crowded city with shops and cargo, not families farming for themselves.
whyNot.B: Private sellers fill the bridge and riverbanks, so trade was not banned.
whyNot.D: The bridge and streets are packed with people.

practice.hint: Count the shops, stalls, carts, and boats.

practice.stem: Which of the following most directly contributed to the growth of cities like the one shown in the painting?

options.A: The Mongol conquest that united northern and southern China
options.B: The spread of Neo-Confucian ideas about family duty
options.C: The Song government's ban on trade with foreign merchants
options.D: The spread of fast-ripening Champa rice from Vietnam

practice.explanation: Fast-ripening Champa rice came from what is now Vietnam. In warm, wet parts of southern China, farmers could grow two crops a year. More food supported more people, and cities grew.

whyNot.A: The Mongols conquered the Song in 1279, more than 150 years after this painting was made.
whyNot.B: Neo-Confucianism shaped ideas about family and government, but it did not grow the food that cities needed.
whyNot.C: The Song government encouraged and taxed foreign trade. It did not ban it.

practice.hint: What change outside the city could help it feed more people?

practice.stem: The large cargo boat on the river is best understood in the context of

options.A: Song China's rivers and canals, including the Grand Canal
options.B: the Song navy's war against Japanese pirates on the coast of China
options.C: the voyages of the Ming admiral Zheng He to the Indian Ocean
options.D: the use of camel caravans to carry goods across Central Asia

practice.explanation: Rivers and canals, like the Grand Canal, linked China's south and north. Boats carried rice and other goods to the growing cities.

whyNot.B: The boat is a river cargo boat in a city, not a warship fighting pirates.
whyNot.C: Zheng He's voyages took place in the early 1400s, about three hundred years after this painting.
whyNot.D: Camel caravans crossed deserts; this boat is moving goods on a river.

practice.hint: How did goods travel between China's north and south?

practice.stem: Al-Ghazali's main claim in the passage is that

options.A: Islamic law should be replaced by the teachings of the Greek philosophers
options.B: scholars should spend their lives teaching in famous colleges in Baghdad
options.C: Sufi practice offers a path to knowing God that study alone cannot provide
options.D: Muslims should follow the reasoning of the theologians rather than personal experience

practice.explanation: Al-Ghazali says Sufism is about "experiences rather than definitions." Learning about Sufism was not enough. He also had to practice it and examine his own motives, so he gave up his famous teaching job.

whyNot.A: Al-Ghazali says philosophers could not make the Sufis' way any better. So he is not picking philosophy over religious law.
whyNot.B: He gave up his teaching post in Baghdad because he thought it was driven by pride.
whyNot.D: He says direct experience of God, not argument alone, brought him certainty.

practice.hint: What did al-Ghazali give up, and what did he choose instead?

practice.stem: Sufi practices like those al-Ghazali describes most directly contributed to which development from c. 1200 to c. 1450?

options.A: The spread of Islam into South and Southeast Asia and Africa
options.B: The end of the Abbasid Caliphate's rule over the Muslim lands of Spain
options.C: The Crusaders' capture of Jerusalem from Muslim rulers
options.D: The adoption of Confucian ideas by the Delhi Sultanate

practice.explanation: Sufi teachers traveled far, built communities, and often blended Islam with local customs. Along with trade and new Muslim rulers, their work helped Islam spread in South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Africa.

whyNot.B: Muslim Spain had broken away from the Abbasids in the 700s, long before this period.
whyNot.C: The Crusaders captured Jerusalem by war in 1099; Sufi practices did not cause it.
whyNot.D: The Delhi Sultanate did not adopt Confucian ideas.

practice.hint: Sufis traveled and taught. What happened in the places they went?

practice.stem: The approach to religion that al-Ghazali describes is most similar to which of the following?

options.A: Neo-Confucianism in China
options.B: The doctrine of papal supremacy over kings
options.C: The Bhakti movement in South Asia
options.D: Inca worship of the sun as the royal ancestor

practice.explanation: Many Sufi and Bhakti teachers stressed personal devotion and love for God. Both taught that a person could reach God through the heart, though their followers could also value study, ritual, and religious rules.

whyNot.A: Neo-Confucianism was about how people should treat their families and rulers. It was not about feeling close to God.
whyNot.B: That claim is about the power of the Church over kings, not personal devotion.
whyNot.D: This choice is about royal ancestry and power, while the passage focuses on a personal religious path.

practice.hint: Decide what al-Ghazali values most in religious practice. Then look for a movement with the same focus.

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a similarity between the two sources?

options.A: Both say believers should ignore the ancient Greek philosophers.
options.B: Both say reason and philosophy can work together with religious faith.
options.C: Both say religious law should be replaced by human reason.
options.D: Both say the study of philosophy should be left to priests.

practice.explanation: Ibn Rushd says Islamic law tells people to study creation with reason. Aquinas says reason should "minister to faith." Both saw reason and faith as partners.

whyNot.A: Source 1 says to read the Ancients' books, and Source 2 uses the authority of philosophers.
whyNot.C: Both say reason serves religion; neither says it should replace religious law.
whyNot.D: Neither source limits philosophy to priests.

practice.hint: What does each writer say reason and philosophy can do for faith?

practice.stem: Which difference in emphasis between the two sources is most clearly supported?

options.A: Source 1 rejects the Greek philosophers; Source 2 rejects the Bible as a guide to truth.
options.B: Source 1 stresses a duty to use reason; Source 2 stresses truths known by revelation.
options.C: Source 1 wants judges to decide what may be studied; Source 2 leaves that to the pope.
options.D: Source 1 is written for Christians; Source 2 is written for Muslims.

practice.explanation: Both writers value reason. Ibn Rushd stresses that Islamic law calls for the study of philosophy. Aquinas stresses that some truths are beyond reason and must be revealed by God. The sources differ in emphasis; they do not fully disagree.

whyNot.A: Source 1 tells readers to study the Ancients' books, and Source 2 depends on the Bible.
whyNot.C: Neither source says who decides what may be studied. Both discuss how reason relates to faith.
whyNot.D: Ibn Rushd wrote about Islamic law for Muslims, and Aquinas wrote for Christians.

practice.hint: Find the words "exceed human reason" in Source 2. What does Source 1 focus on instead?

practice.stem: Ideas like those of Ibn Rushd most likely reached Christian scholars such as Aquinas through

options.A: Mongol envoys who carried books from Baghdad to Paris
options.B: Portuguese sailors returning from voyages around Africa
options.C: Chinese merchants who sold printed books in European ports
options.D: Latin translations of Arabic books made in Spain

practice.explanation: Scholars in Spain and Sicily turned Arabic books into Latin. These included Ibn Rushd's notes on Aristotle. Thinkers like Aquinas read them and argued about them.

whyNot.A: The Mongols did not carry Arabic philosophy books to Paris.
whyNot.B: Portuguese voyages around Africa came in the late 1400s, after Aquinas died in 1274.
whyNot.C: Chinese merchants did not sell books in European ports in this period.

practice.hint: Muslim Spain and Christian Europe were neighbors. How did ideas cross between them?

practice.stem: The passage best illustrates which characteristic of the Delhi Sultanate?

options.A: It was a Hindu kingdom that welcomed Buddhist monks from China.
options.B: It was a Muslim state that ruled over a large Hindu population.
options.C: It was a province of the Abbasid Caliphate ruled from Baghdad.
options.D: It was a Mongol khanate ruled from Persia.

practice.explanation: Muslim Turkic armies conquered northern India around 1200. Their sultans ruled from Delhi. Most of their subjects stayed Hindu.

whyNot.A: The sultan is a Muslim ruler; the passage describes a mosque built where a Hindu temple had stood.
whyNot.C: Delhi was an independent sultanate. Mongol forces ended Abbasid rule in Baghdad in 1258.
whyNot.D: The Delhi sultans fought off Mongol attacks. They were not ruled by the Mongols.

practice.hint: What religion did the sultan follow? What had stood on the mosque's site before?

practice.stem: The sultan's practice of giving high offices to foreigners helps explain how

options.A: scholars like Ibn Battuta could find posts across Dar al-Islam
options.B: Hindu priests came to control most of the Delhi Sultanate's government
options.C: Chinese officials introduced civil service exams to northern India
options.D: European knights became the main soldiers of the sultan's army

practice.explanation: Training in Islamic law gave scholars skills that many Muslim states valued. So a scholar from Morocco could work as a judge in Delhi. Ibn Battuta did just that.

whyNot.B: The sultan favored foreign Muslims; the passage does not say Hindu priests ran the government.
whyNot.C: The Delhi Sultanate did not adopt Chinese civil service exams.
whyNot.D: European knights did not serve as the sultan's army.

practice.hint: Ibn Battuta was a foreigner. What job did he get in Delhi?

practice.stem: The building of a mosque on the site of a temple, described in the second paragraph, is best understood in the context of

options.A: the conversion of most Indians to Islam by the early 1200s
options.B: the Mughal emperors' policy of welcoming many religions
options.C: Buddhism's replacement of Hinduism as India's main religion
options.D: rulers' use of buildings to display their power and faith

practice.explanation: After Muslim armies took Delhi, they turned a temple site into a mosque. This displayed the new rulers' power and faith, and it could stir conflict with Hindu subjects. It does not show how every sultan treated his subjects.

whyNot.A: Most people in India stayed Hindu; they did not convert by the 1200s.
whyNot.B: The Mughal Empire was founded in 1526, long after Ibn Battuta's visit.
whyNot.C: Hinduism stayed India's main religion; Buddhism had declined there.

practice.hint: What message would new rulers send by building a mosque on a temple site?

practice.stem: Abd al-Razzaq's description best supports which claim about Vijayanagara?

options.A: Its merchant councils held more power than the kings who inherited the throne.
options.B: Its rulers lived mainly on tribute from nomadic herders who moved with their flocks.
options.C: Its military power was divided among many independent port cities.
options.D: Its wealth supported a powerful king who ruled a large territory.

practice.explanation: Abd al-Razzaq describes a fertile, crowded country and a very powerful king whose lands stretched from the border of Sri Lanka far to the north. His troop number is a visitor's report, not an exact count. Vijayanagara was one of South Asia's strongest states.

whyNot.A: He calls the king "absolute" and gives him great power. He says nothing about merchant councils ruling.
whyNot.B: He describes a well-farmed, fertile country and busy markets, not nomadic herders paying tribute.
whyNot.C: The country has about three hundred harbors, but one king rules them all, with a huge army.

practice.hint: List what he says about the king, the army, and the markets.

practice.stem: The statement that "the Brahmins hold a rank superior to that of all other men" best reflects the influence of

options.A: the Hindu caste system on social order in South Asia
options.B: Buddhist monasteries that owned most of India's farmland
options.C: Islamic law, which placed scholars above rulers
options.D: Confucian ideas about loyalty between minister and ruler

practice.explanation: In Hindu social tradition, people were born into ranked groups. Brahmins, many of whom were priests or scholars, held the highest religious status. Their actual wealth and power could vary.

whyNot.B: Brahmins were Hindu priests, not Buddhist monks.
whyNot.C: Brahmins were part of the Hindu social order, not Islamic law.
whyNot.D: Confucianism shaped East Asia, not the Hindu kingdom of Vijayanagara.

practice.hint: First decide which religion the Brahmins belonged to. Then ask which choice explains why a whole group was ranked above others.

practice.stem: Vijayanagara's large army and seven rings of walls are best understood in the context of

options.A: attacks by Portuguese warships on the cities of southern India
options.B: the Mongol invasion and conquest of southern India in the 1200s
options.C: rebellions by Buddhist monks against the Hindu kings of the south
options.D: wars with nearby Muslim states such as the Bahmani Sultanate

practice.explanation: Vijayanagara was founded in 1336. It fought many wars with the Bahmani Sultanate to its north. Strong walls and a big army helped it survive.

whyNot.A: The Portuguese did not reach India until 1498, more than 50 years after this visit.
whyNot.B: The Mongols did not conquer southern India.
whyNot.C: Vijayanagara mostly fought nearby Muslim kingdoms, not Buddhist monks.

practice.hint: Who were Vijayanagara's neighbors to the north?

practice.stem: The table best supports which claim about the Mexica Empire?

options.A: It collected its taxes mainly in gold and silver coins.
options.B: It got its cacao and feathers by trading with the Inca Empire.
options.C: It asked its provinces to send tribute once in ten years.
options.D: It drew goods from conquered peoples in different environments.

practice.explanation: A province near the capital sent cloth, paper, cups, and food. A far-off tropical province sent cacao, feathers, and jaguar skins. Tribute brought wealth from many regions.

whyNot.A: The tribute was mostly cloth, food, feathers, and other goods. The Mexica did not use coins.
whyNot.B: The Mexica and Inca did not trade directly. The cacao and feathers came as tribute from Xoconochco.
whyNot.C: The table shows payments every six months or once a year.

practice.hint: Compare what each province sent. Where did each item come from?

practice.stem: The Mexica way of gathering wealth shown in the table differed most from that of the Inca Empire, which

options.A: used cacao beans as money when collecting tribute
options.B: kept its tribute records in painted books like the codex
options.C: relied heavily on the mit'a, a system of required labor service
options.D: depended on merchants called pochteca to bring in tribute

practice.explanation: Both empires demanded goods and some labor. But labor service was especially central to the Inca state. Under the mit'a, communities took turns sending workers to state farms, roads, and buildings.

whyNot.A: Cacao beans were used like money in Mesoamerica, not in the Andes.
whyNot.B: The Incas kept records on knotted cords called quipus, not in painted books.
whyNot.D: Pochteca were Mexica traders. The Inca state moved goods mostly through labor service and storehouses, not merchants.

practice.hint: The table shows goods. What else, besides goods, could an empire demand from the people it ruled?

practice.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the codex as evidence of Mexica tribute?

options.A: It was made after the conquest, partly for Spanish officials.
options.B: It was painted by Spanish artists who had not met any Mexica people.
options.C: It was written centuries after the Mexica Empire had fallen.
options.D: It lists luxury goods such as gold and jewels but leaves out everyday goods like cloth.

practice.explanation: The codex was made around 1541 for Spanish officials. Its notes are in Spanish. The makers may have changed or simplified older records for these readers.

whyNot.B: The note says it was painted by Indigenous artists.
whyNot.C: It was made about 1541, twenty years after the conquest.
whyNot.D: The table lists everyday goods such as cloaks and maize as well as luxury goods.

practice.hint: Read the note under the table. When and for whom was the codex made?

practice.stem: Díaz's description best supports which claim about the Mexica capital?

options.A: It had little trade because the Mexica people depended on farming.
options.B: It used gold coins as the main money in its markets.
options.C: It had large, orderly markets with goods from many regions.
options.D: Its market sold mostly food grown in the nearby countryside.

practice.explanation: Díaz was amazed by the crowds and the many kinds of goods. He also praised the market's order. The Mexica capital was a rich center of trade.

whyNot.A: Díaz describes a huge market with every kind of merchandise.
whyNot.B: Traders used cacao, cotton cloaks, and quills of gold dust, not coins.
whyNot.D: Díaz lists gold, silver, feathers, mantles, and cacao, and says the market held every sort of merchandise in New Spain.

practice.hint: How does Díaz describe the market's size and order?

practice.stem: Díaz most likely compared the market to the fairs of Medina del Campo in order to

options.A: argue that Spain should copy Mexica laws about trade
options.B: show that Spanish merchants had set up the market
options.C: help Spanish readers picture the market's size and order
options.D: complain that the Mexica market was less organized than Spain's

practice.explanation: Díaz wrote for Spanish readers who had never seen Mexico. A famous Spanish fair gave them something familiar to picture. The comparison helped them see how large and orderly the Mexica market was.

whyNot.A: Díaz is describing the market, not arguing for new laws in Spain.
whyNot.B: The market existed before the Spanish arrived; Díaz was seeing it for the first time.
whyNot.D: Díaz praises the market's "good order and control"; he does not call it disorganized.

practice.hint: Who was Díaz writing for? What would they already know?

practice.stem: Goods from across the region were available in the market mainly because

options.A: Spanish ships had recently brought goods from Europe to Mexico
options.B: the Inca Empire sent yearly caravans of goods from Peru to Mexico
options.C: the Mexica required foreign merchants to sell their goods in Tenochtitlan
options.D: the Mexica took in tribute, and their merchants traded far away

practice.explanation: Tribute from conquered lands poured into the capital. Mexica merchants, called pochteca, also traveled far to trade. Both brought goods to the city's markets.

whyNot.A: Díaz was describing the market in 1519, when the Spanish had only just arrived.
whyNot.B: The Inca and Mexica empires did not trade directly with each other.
whyNot.C: The Mexica had many markets, and nothing in the passage says merchants were forced to sell in the capital.

practice.hint: How did the Mexica get goods from faraway provinces?

practice.stem: Prescott's main argument in the passage is that

options.A: the Aztecs and Incas ruled their conquered peoples in nearly the same way
options.B: the Aztecs treated conquered peoples better than the Incas did
options.C: the Incas won conquered peoples' loyalty; the Aztecs ruled by fear
options.D: neither empire tried to expand by conquering its neighbors

practice.explanation: Prescott contrasts "the principle of fear" with "the principle of love." He says the Incas welcomed conquered peoples into the empire. He says the Aztecs held theirs down by force.

whyNot.A: Prescott says the two policies formed a "striking" contrast.
whyNot.B: Prescott says the opposite: the Aztecs were harsher.
whyNot.D: Prescott says both empires conquered their neighbors. He says the Incas did it "with equal pertinacity," which means just as stubbornly.

practice.hint: Read the last sentence of the passage.

practice.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most challenge Prescott's claim about the Incas?

options.A: The Incas built storehouses of food along their roads.
options.B: The Incas gave gifts of fine cloth to the local leaders who stayed loyal.
options.C: The Incas recorded tribute and labor on knotted cords called quipus.
options.D: The Incas forced conquered peoples to move and spied on them.

practice.explanation: Prescott says the Incas ruled with "parental solicitude," or loving care. Forced moves and spying show fear and control instead. That evidence weakens his claim.

whyNot.A: Storehouses could fit Prescott's picture of a caring government.
whyNot.B: Gifts to loyal leaders fit Prescott's picture of winning loyalty.
whyNot.C: Record keeping does not show whether the Incas ruled by love or by fear.

practice.hint: What evidence would make Prescott's kind picture of Inca rule less convincing?

practice.stem: Which of the following developments best supports Prescott's claim that peoples ruled by the Aztecs were "ready to fall asunder"?

options.A: The Mexica built a great temple in Tenochtitlan for their gods.
options.B: Subject peoples such as the Totonacs joined the Spanish in 1519.
options.C: Mexica merchants traveled long distances to trade in distant markets.
options.D: The Mexica capital grew to have well over 100,000 people.

practice.explanation: In 1519 the Totonacs, who paid tribute to the Mexica, joined Cortés. The Mexica's old enemies in Tlaxcala did too. Many unhappy peoples fought on the Spanish side.

whyNot.A: A temple shows Mexica religion and power, not weak loyalty.
whyNot.C: Long-distance trade does not show that subject peoples wanted to break away.
whyNot.D: A large capital shows the empire's strength, not its weakness.

practice.hint: Which choice is evidence about how conquered peoples felt toward Mexica rule?

practice.stem: Ibn Battuta's account best supports which claim about the East African coast?

options.A: Its towns were run by visiting Arab sailors, not local rulers.
options.B: Its towns were Muslim trading centers linked to the Indian Ocean.
options.C: Its people refused to trade with merchants who arrived by sea.
options.D: Its towns were ruled by governors sent from China.

practice.explanation: Mogadishu was full of merchants. Kilwa's sultan followed the Quran. The Swahili coast was a chain of Muslim trading towns facing the Indian Ocean.

whyNot.A: The passage names Kilwa's own sultan, and local hosts in Mogadishu controlled trade with visiting merchants.
whyNot.C: Mogadishu's people met every ship and sold the merchants' goods for them.
whyNot.D: Chinese fleets visited East Africa only briefly, in the early 1400s, and did not rule its towns.

practice.hint: What were the people of Mogadishu? What religion did Kilwa's sultan follow?

practice.stem: The gold trade that brought gold dust to Sofala most directly helped which inland African state grow powerful?

options.A: Great Zimbabwe
options.B: The Mali Empire
options.C: The Kingdom of Kongo
options.D: The Hausa kingdoms

practice.explanation: Gold from inland southern Africa went to Sofala and then north to Kilwa. Great Zimbabwe gained wealth from this trade between the gold regions and the coast. Farming and cattle also supported the state.

whyNot.B: Mali was in West Africa; its gold went north across the Sahara.
whyNot.C: Kongo was in west-central Africa, near the Atlantic, far from Sofala.
whyNot.D: The Hausa kingdoms were in West Africa, south of the Sahara.

practice.hint: Find Sofala on a map of East Africa. Which state was inland from it?

practice.stem: The sultan's practice described in the last paragraph best reflects

options.A: the spread of Christianity from Ethiopia to the coast
options.B: the influence of Confucian ideas brought by Chinese traders on African rulers
options.C: the adoption of Islam by rulers on the Swahili coast
options.D: the rise of Hindu temples in East African ports

practice.explanation: The sultan gave a fifth of his war booty to charity, following the Quran. Trade with Arabia and Persia brought Islam to the Swahili coast. Many rulers there became Muslim.

whyNot.A: The sultan follows the Koran, not Christian teaching.
whyNot.B: Confucian ideas did not shape the rulers of the Swahili coast.
whyNot.D: The sultan follows Islamic rules about giving to charity.

practice.hint: What rule is the sultan following, and what does that suggest about his authority?

practice.stem: Randall-MacIver's main argument is that Great Zimbabwe was

options.A: built in ancient times by settlers from the Middle East
options.B: built by Portuguese traders in the 1500s
options.C: built in the Middle Ages by Africans of the region
options.D: built by North African merchants in the Middle Ages

practice.explanation: Randall-MacIver says the objects found were African or medieval imports. He says the builders' crafts matched those of local people. So Africans built it in the Middle Ages.

whyNot.A: He calls that "popular opinion" and says the evidence does not support it.
whyNot.B: He dates the building to the 1300s or 1400s and links it to local African peoples, not the Portuguese.
whyNot.D: He links the builders' crafts to local African peoples. Imported objects show trade, not foreign builders.

practice.hint: What did "popular opinion" say? Does he agree?

practice.stem: Which evidence does Randall-MacIver use to date the Elliptical Temple?

options.A: Arabic glass and Chinese porcelain found in the cement of the building
options.B: Writings left on the walls by ancient Egyptian and Greek travelers
options.C: Records kept by the Portuguese captains who built the walls
options.D: Stories told by the Arab merchants who first lived inside it

practice.explanation: Medieval Arabic glass and Chinese porcelain were found inside the Temple's cement foundation. Randall-MacIver argued that the building could not be older than these objects, so he dated it to the 1300s or later. Later archaeologists refined his dates.

whyNot.B: He mentions no ancient writing on the walls.
whyNot.C: Portuguese records begin in the 1500s, and the Portuguese did not build the walls.
whyNot.D: He says Arab merchants traded with Zimbabwe's people, not that they lived inside the enclosure.

practice.hint: Reread the third paragraph. What was found, and where?

practice.stem: The trade described in the last paragraph connected Great Zimbabwe most directly to

options.A: the trans-Saharan caravan routes of Mali
options.B: the Silk Roads linking China and the Mediterranean
options.C: Swahili coast city-states such as Kilwa and Sofala
options.D: Atlantic ports run by Portuguese merchants

practice.explanation: Great Zimbabwe's gold went to traders on the coast. They shipped it across the Indian Ocean. Sofala and Kilwa grew rich as the link between inland Africa and the sea.

whyNot.A: The trans-Saharan routes linked West Africa to North Africa, far from Zimbabwe.
whyNot.B: The Silk Roads were overland routes across Asia.
whyNot.D: Portuguese traders arrived on the East African coast only around 1500.

practice.hint: Merchants "from the east coast" bought the gold. Which cities were there?

practice.stem: The scribe Isaac's purpose in producing the book was most likely to

options.A: persuade Ethiopians to convert from Christianity to Judaism
options.B: encourage a woman to take the throne of Ethiopia
options.C: support the claim that Ethiopia's kings ruled by right
options.D: warn Ethiopia's kings against trading with Arabia

practice.explanation: Isaac says he worked "for the glory of the King of Ethiopia." The book traces the kings back to Solomon. It says their right to rule lasts "for ever."

whyNot.A: The book uses the story of Solomon to honor Ethiopia's Christian kings; it does not ask anyone to change religion.
whyNot.B: The passage says a woman "shall nevermore reign."
whyNot.D: The passage does not mention trade with Arabia.

practice.hint: Read the scribe's closing note. Whose glory did he work for?

practice.stem: The book's claims about the royal line are best understood in the context of

options.A: the Mamluk Sultanate's conquest of Ethiopia in the 1260s
options.B: a new dynasty's claim to the throne after it took power in 1270
options.C: the Byzantine emperor's control over Ethiopia's Christian church
options.D: the conversion of Ethiopia's kings to Islam in the 1200s

practice.explanation: In 1270 a new dynasty, the Solomonic dynasty, replaced the Zagwe kings. The new kings claimed descent from Solomon. That claim made them look like the true rulers.

whyNot.A: The Mamluks ruled Egypt and Syria. They never conquered Ethiopia.
whyNot.C: Ethiopia's church looked to the Christian patriarch in Alexandria, Egypt, not to the Byzantine emperor. The book is about kings, not church control.
whyNot.D: Ethiopia's kings stayed Christian. The scribe Isaac was a Christian who praised Christian kings.

practice.hint: The note says the book was not translated "in the days of Zagua." Why might a new dynasty want it?

practice.stem: The Ethiopian kings' use of religion to support their rule, as shown in the passage, was most similar to

options.A: Chinese emperors' claim to rule by the Mandate of Heaven
options.B: the English barons' use of Magna Carta to limit the king
options.C: the Golden Bull's rule that princes elect the emperor
options.D: the Inca practice of moving conquered peoples

practice.explanation: Both Ethiopian and Chinese rulers said a higher power approved their rule. Ethiopia's kings pointed to Solomon and the Ark. China's emperors pointed to the Mandate of Heaven.

whyNot.B: Magna Carta limited a king's power; it did not use religion to justify a royal line.
whyNot.C: The Golden Bull set rules for electing the emperor. It did not use a religious story to show that one family had the right to rule.
whyNot.D: Moving peoples was a way to control conquered lands, not a religious claim to rule.

practice.hint: Which other rulers said a divine power chose them?

practice.stem: Hugh Miller's duties, as described in the survey, are characteristic of

options.A: slavery, in which workers were bought and sold
options.B: serfdom, in which peasants owed labor and fees to a lord
options.C: wage labor, in which workers were paid for their work
options.D: the guild system, in which craftsmen trained apprentices

practice.explanation: Hugh held land from the abbot. In return, he owed three days of work a week, payments in food such as hens and eggs, and fees like merchet and heriot. These duties show serfdom.

whyNot.A: The survey lists Hugh among the villeins, who held land and owed duties with it. Those details point to serfdom.
whyNot.C: Hugh works for the lord without pay three days a week.
whyNot.D: Hugh is a farmer who owes services, not a craftsman training apprentices.

practice.hint: What does Hugh owe the abbot each week and on special occasions?

practice.stem: The survey best supports which claim about the Church in medieval Europe?

options.A: The Church refused to own land and lived on gifts instead.
options.B: The Church held large estates worked by peasants.
options.C: The Church freed the serfs who lived on its lands.
options.D: The Church paid wages to the peasants who farmed its fields.

practice.explanation: The lord of this manor is an abbot, the head of a monastery. Churches and monasteries owned huge amounts of land. Serfs did much of the work on it.

whyNot.A: The abbot of Peterborough holds the whole manor.
whyNot.C: Villeins on the abbot's manor still owed work and fees.
whyNot.D: The listed work was owed as a duty. The survey does not describe wages for it.

practice.hint: Who is the lord of this manor?

practice.stem: Farm labor on the manor described here differed most from farm labor in Song China in that Song China

options.A: relied mainly on enslaved war captives from the steppe
options.B: relied mainly on the mit'a, a system of rotating labor service
options.C: relied mainly on peasants bound to Buddhist monasteries
options.D: relied mainly on free peasants rather than serfs

practice.explanation: In Europe, many peasants were serfs who owed work to a lord. Song China depended mostly on free peasants. They paid taxes to the state and could sell their crops.

whyNot.A: Song farms were worked mostly by free peasant families, not by enslaved captives.
whyNot.B: The mit'a was an Inca labor system in the Andes, not a Chinese one.
whyNot.C: Buddhist monasteries owned some land in China, but most Song farmers were free peasants.

practice.hint: Were Song farmers bound to a lord?

practice.stem: Boniface VIII's main claim in the passage is that

options.A: the pope should obey the decisions of Europe's kings
options.B: church and government should be kept separate
options.C: each kingdom should choose its own head of the Church
options.D: kings must be under the authority of the pope

practice.explanation: Boniface says both "swords" belong to the Church. In his view, kings must use their power at the priest's command, so the pope stands above them.

whyNot.A: Boniface says the opposite. Kings' power must be "subjected to," or placed under, the Church's power.
whyNot.B: He says both swords belong to the Church, so he does not want them separate.
whyNot.C: He says every person must submit to "the bishop of Rome," the pope.

practice.hint: Who holds the two swords, according to Boniface?

practice.stem: The decree is best understood in the context of

options.A: conflicts between popes and kings over who held power
options.B: the Great Schism, when rival popes ruled from Rome and Avignon
options.C: the crusades to win back Jerusalem from Muslim rulers
options.D: the split between the Catholic and Orthodox churches in 1054

practice.explanation: Boniface wrote this during a fight with King Philip IV of France. Philip had taxed the French clergy. Popes and kings often clashed over power in this period.

whyNot.B: The Great Schism began in 1378, more than 70 years after this decree.
whyNot.C: Popes did call crusades, but this decree is about the power of kings, not about Jerusalem.
whyNot.D: That split happened in 1054, long before this decree. It was about the churches of East and West, not about popes and kings.

practice.hint: Who was the pope arguing with in 1302?

practice.stem: Which development soon after 1302 most clearly showed the limits of the claims in the decree?

options.A: Philip IV's agents seized Boniface, and the popes later moved to Avignon.
options.B: The Holy Roman Emperor let the pope choose the next German king.
options.C: The French king agreed to stop taxing the clergy of France.
options.D: Crusaders retook Jerusalem and handed it over to the pope.

practice.explanation: In 1303 Philip's agents seized Boniface at Anagni, and he died soon after. From 1309 the popes lived in Avignon, under strong French influence. Kings were gaining power over popes.

whyNot.B: German princes, not the pope, chose the king. The Golden Bull of 1356 made this rule official.
whyNot.C: Philip IV kept taxing the French clergy. That quarrel is part of what led to the decree.
whyNot.D: Crusaders did not retake Jerusalem in this period. Their last stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291.

practice.hint: What happened between Boniface and the French king in 1303?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 orders Jews to become Christians; Source 2 forbids anyone from converting Jews.
options.B: Source 1 shields Jews from violence; Source 2 makes them cancel crusaders' interest.
options.C: Source 1 calls for a crusade; Source 2 protects Jewish cemeteries.
options.D: Source 1 limits Jewish moneylending; Source 2 protects Jewish festivals.

practice.explanation: Source 1 forbids beating Jews or forcing them to convert. Source 2 forces Jews to give up interest owed by crusaders. The Church both protected and burdened Jews.

whyNot.A: Source 1 says no one may force Jews to be baptized.
whyNot.C: It is the reverse: Source 2 calls for a crusade, and Source 1 protects Jewish cemeteries.
whyNot.D: It is the reverse: Source 2 deals with Jewish lending, and Source 1 protects Jewish festivals.

practice.hint: Compare what each source allows, requires, or forbids.

practice.stem: The reference to Jews collecting interest in Source 2 is best understood in the context of

options.A: the Hanseatic League's control of trade in the Baltic Sea
options.B: the Church's ban on Christians charging interest on loans
options.C: laws in Europe that let Jews own most of the farmland
options.D: the Crusaders' capture of the Christian city of Constantinople in 1204

practice.explanation: Church teaching condemned charging interest on loans, but some Christians lent money anyway. Some Jews also worked as lenders. Local rules often limited the other jobs open to Jews, but these rules varied by place.

whyNot.A: The Hanseatic League of north German trading towns formed later, in the 1300s, and it does not explain lending to crusaders.
whyNot.C: Jewish land rights varied by place. The source gives no sign that Jews owned most farmland.
whyNot.D: The capture of Constantinople in 1204 was a war between Christians. It does not explain why Jews lent money.

practice.hint: What did Church teaching say about charging interest?

practice.stem: The kinds of attacks on Jews that Source 1 forbids were part of a pattern that later included

options.A: the expulsion of Jews from England in 1290 and from France in 1306
options.B: the Church's new decision to let Christians charge interest on their loans
options.C: a law in the Holy Roman Empire that freed Jews from paying special taxes
options.D: the invitation of Jewish refugees to settle in England after 1300

practice.explanation: Jews in medieval Europe faced attacks, special taxes, and expulsions. England expelled its Jews in 1290, and France ordered a major expulsion in 1306. These actions show the limits of the protection promised in Source 1.

whyNot.B: The Church kept its ban on Christians charging interest throughout this period.
whyNot.C: Rulers kept collecting special taxes from Jewish communities.
whyNot.D: England did not let Jews return until the 1650s, long after this period.

practice.hint: What did some European kings do to Jewish communities in the late 1200s and early 1300s?

exam.title: Unit 1 Practice Exam: The Global Tapestry
exam.directions: Each set of questions refers to a source: a primary source, a historian's writing, an image, or data. For each question, choose the best answer. Use the source and your knowledge of world history from c. 1200 to c. 1450. There is no penalty for guessing. Some sources use historical labels or insulting descriptions of other peoples and religions; these words show the writers' views.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the rulers of Srivijaya gained wealth and power mainly by

options.A: conquering large rice-farming regions on the mainland of Asia
options.B: controlling a narrow sea route and making ships stop there
options.C: mining gold and silver to make coins for trade
options.D: sending settlers to build colonies on India's coast

rationales.A: Incorrect. The passage is about control of the sea and trade, not about conquering farmland on the mainland.
rationales.B: Correct. Zhao says Srivijaya controls "the straits" that ships must pass through. If a ship tries to sail past, Srivijaya's boats attack it.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Gold and silver came in from foreign traders. The passage does not say Srivijaya mined metals or made coins.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The passage says foreign traders came to Srivijaya. It does not say Srivijaya sent settlers to India.

questions.explanation: Srivijaya controlled ports and straits on the main sea routes between the Indian Ocean and China. Zhao says its ships forced passing traders to stop. Srivijaya grew rich by taxing this trade.

questions.stem: The goods that foreign traders gave in exchange at Srivijaya, such as porcelain, silk, and iron, best reflect which development in Song China?

options.A: The use of paper money alongside metal coins in trade
options.B: Growing production of manufactured goods for trade
options.C: The spread of Champa rice and other improvements in farming
options.D: The selection of officials through exams on Confucian texts

rationales.A: Incorrect. Song China did use paper money, but porcelain, silk, and iron are trade goods, not money.
rationales.B: Correct. Song workshops made large amounts of porcelain, silk cloth, and iron. Merchants shipped these goods to Southeast Asia and beyond.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Champa rice did help Song farmers, but porcelain, silk, and iron were made in workshops, not grown in fields.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Song China did choose officials by exams, but exams do not explain the goods that traders carried.

questions.explanation: The Song economy became very commercial. Workshops and kilns made huge amounts of porcelain, silk, and iron. Merchants sold these goods across the Indian Ocean world.

questions.stem: Srivijaya's tribute missions to the Chinese court, described in the last paragraph, are best understood in the context of

options.A: the Mongol practice of making conquered lands send soldiers for its wars
options.B: the spread of Islam into Sumatra by merchants from Arabia and Persia
options.C: a Song plan to conquer the ports of Southeast Asia and rule them directly
options.D: China's tribute system, in which rulers sent gifts to gain trade

rationales.A: Incorrect. The missions took place from the 960s to the 1090s, long before the Mongols conquered the Song in 1279.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The missions honored the emperor and a Buddhist temple. They have nothing to do with Islam.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Song did not try to rule Srivijaya. Srivijaya's rulers chose to send the missions.
rationales.D: Correct. Rulers of nearby states sent gifts, called tribute, to the Chinese emperor. In return they received gifts, the right to trade, and the emperor's recognition.

questions.explanation: Sending tribute kept a ruler on good terms with the Chinese emperor. The ruler gained trade and prestige. The emperor gained foreign rulers' recognition of his high status.

questions.stem: Zhu Xi's main criticism of Buddhists and Daoists in the passage is that they

options.A: turn away from family and social duties, the basis of morality
options.B: rely too heavily on written exams to choose government officials
options.C: encourage merchants to seek profit instead of serving the state
options.D: teach that rulers may govern without the Mandate of Heaven

rationales.A: Correct. Zhu Xi says Buddhists and Daoists "discard human relationships." For him, morality lives in daily duties. A son obeys his father, and a minister is loyal to his ruler.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The passage does not discuss exams. Zhu Xi criticizes how Buddhists and Daoists treat family ties.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The passage is about family and social relationships, not merchants or profit.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The passage does not mention the Mandate of Heaven.

questions.explanation: Many Buddhist and Daoist monks left their families for monasteries. Zhu Xi called this a mistake. He said the moral Way is lived in everyday family and social ties.

questions.stem: The ideas in the passage most directly influenced which of the following developments in East Asia?

options.A: The replacement of Confucian schools in Korea by Buddhist monasteries
options.B: Song China's adoption of Theravada Buddhism
options.C: An end to the hiring of scholar-officials in China
options.D: The use of Zhu Xi's teachings on China's civil service exams

rationales.A: Incorrect. Korea's Joseon kings, who took power in 1392, promoted Neo-Confucian learning and limited Buddhist monasteries.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Theravada Buddhism spread in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia, not as China's official religion.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Chinese emperors kept choosing scholar-officials through exams.
rationales.D: Correct. In 1313, Yuan rulers made Zhu Xi's explanations of the Four Books, key Confucian texts, the standard guide for China's civil service exams, which began again in 1315. His ideas stayed central to the exams until 1905.

questions.explanation: Zhu Xi was a leading Neo-Confucian thinker. Under the Yuan dynasty, his explanations of the Four Books became the standard guide for China's civil service exams. His teachings also spread to Korea and Japan.

questions.stem: Zhu Xi's ideas in the passage are best understood in the context of

options.A: the arrival of Christian missionaries at the court of the Song emperor
options.B: the Mongol conquest that ended the Song dynasty in 1279
options.C: a Confucian response to the long popularity of Buddhism in China
options.D: the spread of Islam into China through Arab merchants in Quanzhou

rationales.A: Incorrect. The passage is about Zhu Xi's response to Buddhism and Daoism, not to Christianity.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Zhu Xi died in 1200, decades before the Mongols ended the Song dynasty.
rationales.C: Correct. Buddhism had been popular in China for centuries. Neo-Confucians like Zhu Xi borrowed some Buddhist ideas about the mind. But they said family and social duties come first.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Muslim merchants did live in Song ports, but Zhu Xi is answering Buddhism and Daoism, not Islam.

questions.explanation: Buddhism had shaped Chinese life for about a thousand years. Neo-Confucianism was partly an answer to it. It kept family duty at the center of life.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Arnold's argument about how Islam spread in Sumatra and nearby islands?

options.A: It spread mainly because Muslim armies from India conquered the island.
options.B: It spread chiefly through the work of merchants and religious teachers.
options.C: It reached the hill peoples first and the coastal towns much later.
options.D: It spread after Sumatra's rulers began paying tribute to Mecca.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Arnold admits that the sword was sometimes used, but he says nothing about armies from India. He stresses traders and preachers.
rationales.B: Correct. Arnold credits "Saracen merchants," missionaries sent from Mecca, and traders who married local women. He says "preaching and persuasion rather than force" were the main features.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Arnold says the reverse: the townspeople of Parlak were Muslim, while "the hill-people" were not.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Sharif of Mecca sent missionaries. The passage does not say that Sumatra paid tribute to Mecca.

questions.explanation: Arnold stresses trade, marriage, and religious teaching. He admits that force was sometimes used, but he gives peaceful work the larger role. Traders married local women and learned the language, and missionaries persuaded rulers to convert.

questions.stem: Arnold uses Ibn Battuta's report about legal experts from Persia and an embassy to Delhi as evidence that

options.A: Persian armies had conquered Sumatra by the middle of the 1300s
options.B: the sultans of Delhi ruled Sumatra as a province of their empire
options.C: Ibn Battuta converted the ruler of Samudra to Islam in 1345
options.D: Samudra's ruler had ties with other parts of the Islamic world

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Persians at the court were legal scholars, not soldiers.
rationales.B: Incorrect. An embassy is a diplomatic visit. It does not mean that Delhi ruled Sumatra.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The ruler Ibn Battuta met was already a Muslim when Ibn Battuta arrived.
rationales.D: Correct. Arnold says these details show "that Sumatra was already in touch with several parts of the Muhammadan world."

questions.explanation: Legal experts came from Persia, and a noble went to Delhi as an ambassador. Arnold uses these facts to show that Samudra's Muslim court had ties across Dar al-Islam, the wider Muslim world.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen Arnold's argument about how Islam spread?

options.A: In West Africa, too, Islam spread first among traders and town rulers, mostly without conquest.
options.B: Muslim armies conquered most of Spain within a few years in the early 700s.
options.C: The ruler of Samudra made war on his non-Muslim neighbors until they paid him tribute.
options.D: The Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of Majapahit was the strongest power on Java in the 1300s.

rationales.A: Correct. If Islam spread the same peaceful way in another trading region, Arnold's claim about traders and missionaries looks stronger. In West Africa, rulers in places like Mali became Muslim through contact with merchants.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Conquest in Spain says nothing in favor of trade spreading Islam in Sumatra. If anything, it points the other way.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Wars to force neighbors to submit would weaken Arnold's claim, not strengthen it. Arnold himself admits that "sometimes indeed the sword has been drawn."
rationales.D: Incorrect. The strength of a Hindu-Buddhist kingdom on Java tells us nothing about how Islam spread in Sumatra.

questions.explanation: Arnold argues that merchants and teachers did more than armies to spread Islam in Sumatra. Evidence that Islam spread the same way in another trading region would make his case stronger.

questions.stem: Kabir's main point in the poems is that

options.A: Hindus should give up their beliefs and convert to Islam
options.B: God is found through inner devotion, not temples or rituals
options.C: high-caste people are closer to God than low-caste people
options.D: true seekers of God must leave society and live as monks

rationales.A: Incorrect. Kabir calls himself the child of both Allah and Ram. He does not ask Hindus to convert.
rationales.B: Correct. Kabir says God is "beside thee," not "in temple nor in mosque," and tells listeners to "look within your heart."
rationales.C: Incorrect. Kabir says "it is needless to ask of a saint the caste to which he belongs."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Kabir says God is not found in "Yoga and renunciation," that is, in giving up ordinary life.

questions.explanation: Kabir taught that God lives in every heart. Holy places, ceremonies, and caste do not bring people closer to God. Love and devotion do.

questions.stem: The ideas expressed in the poems are most closely associated with which religious movement?

options.A: Theravada Buddhism
options.B: Neo-Confucianism
options.C: The Bhakti movement
options.D: Zoroastrianism

rationales.A: Incorrect. Theravada Buddhism honored monks who left ordinary life to meditate. Kabir rejects "renunciation" as the way to God.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Neo-Confucianism grew in China and focused on social relationships, not on finding God in the heart.
rationales.C: Correct. Bhakti poets like Kabir sang in everyday languages about loving devotion to God. Some also rejected caste ranking and empty rituals.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Kabir's poems use Hindu and Muslim names for God, not Zoroastrian ideas.

questions.explanation: These poems reflect the Bhakti movement's focus on loving devotion to God. Kabir, like some other Bhakti poets, also rejected caste ranking.

questions.stem: Kabir's references to both Hindus and Muslims are best understood in the context of which development already under way in South Asia by c. 1450?

options.A: The Vijayanagara kings' defense of Hindu rule in southern India
options.B: The spread of Buddhism from Tibet into the cities of northern India
options.C: Muslim rulers and Sufi teachers living among Hindus in north India
options.D: A ban on Hindu worship issued by the Mongol rulers of Persia

rationales.A: Incorrect. Vijayanagara was a Hindu kingdom in the far south. Kabir lived in Banaras, in the north, and his poems speak to both Hindus and Muslims.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Buddhism had largely faded from northern India by Kabir's time. The poems speak of Hindus and Muslims.
rationales.C: Correct. Muslim sultans had ruled Delhi since the early 1200s. Sufi teachers and Hindu devotional poets lived side by side, and Kabir drew on both traditions.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Mongol rulers of Persia did not govern northern India.

questions.explanation: By Kabir's time, Muslim rulers had governed much of northern India for over two centuries. Hindu and Muslim ideas met there. Kabir uses Hindu and Muslim names for God.

questions.stem: Which purpose of resettlement is most directly supported by Cieza's description of spies among the settlers?

options.A: Reducing resistance in newly conquered provinces
options.B: Punishing criminals by sending them away from the capital
options.C: Increasing food supplies by settling unused farmland
options.D: Giving local chiefs more freedom from imperial officials

rationales.A: Correct. Spies among the settlers reported the conquered people's "conversations and schemes" to the governors and to Cuzco. That helped the Incas stop plots before they became revolts.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Cieza describes the settlers as loyal subjects from peaceful areas, not as criminals.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Incas did sometimes move people to farm new land. But spies watching for plots point to control, not food.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The spies reported to imperial governors. That tightened control over local chiefs instead of loosening it.

questions.explanation: The Incas moved loyal settlers into newly conquered provinces. Spies among them reported possible plots to imperial officials. This helped Inca rulers find and stop rebellions.

questions.stem: Which experience does Cieza give as evidence that the quipus could keep exact records?

options.A: He compared the quipus with written books kept by Inca priests in Cuzco.
options.B: He learned to read the quipus himself while living with the Inca nobles.
options.C: A local lord showed him quipu records of goods given to the Spaniards.
options.D: He checked the quipus against Spanish tax records sent from Mexico.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Cieza describes knotted cords. He does not say he compared them with written books.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Cieza says a local lord explained the quipus to him. He does not say he learned to read them.
rationales.C: Correct. Cieza says the lord Guacarapora showed him records of everything given to the Spaniards. The records were so exact that Cieza "was quite astonished."
rationales.D: Incorrect. The passage does not mention any records from Mexico.

questions.explanation: Cieza admits he doubted the quipus at first. Then a local lord showed him exact records kept in knots. That changed his mind.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of Cieza's account as evidence about Inca rule?

options.A: Cieza relied partly on Inca nobles, who may have played down the harsh side of Inca rule.
options.B: Cieza wrote centuries after the Inca Empire fell, using its ruins as evidence.
options.C: Cieza was an Inca official who wanted to hide the empire's treatment of rebels.
options.D: Cieza did not visit the Andes and based his account on rumors he heard in Spain.

rationales.A: Correct. Inca nobles had reasons to make their former rulers look wise and fair. Conquered peoples who were forced to move might have told a different story.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Cieza wrote about 1550, less than 20 years after the Spanish invasion of 1532, and he talked with living people.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Cieza was a Spanish soldier and writer, not an Inca official.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Cieza traveled in Peru himself and describes his visit to Marcavillca.

questions.explanation: Some of Cieza's informants had belonged to the Inca ruling class. Their accounts may favor their old rulers. Cieza added his own observations, but Inca rule had ended before he arrived, so historians check his account against other evidence.

questions.stem: The Inca policies described in the passage contrast most clearly with the Mexica Empire's greater reliance on

options.A: replacing local rulers with governors and officials sent from the capital
options.B: resettling whole conquered families near the workshops of the capital
options.C: collecting tribute through local rulers they usually left in power
options.D: demanding military service in place of tribute in goods

rationales.A: Incorrect. Mexica rulers sometimes placed governors in conquered towns, but they mostly left local rulers in place. The Incas relied more on officials and settlers sent by the central government.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Moving conquered families was an Inca policy, as the passage shows. The Mexica did not resettle conquered peoples near workshops.
rationales.C: Correct. The Mexica usually left conquered city-states under their own rulers, who collected tribute and sent it on. The Incas also used local leaders, but they did more to reshape conquered areas by moving whole communities.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Mexica demanded soldiers and also goods. Military service did not replace tribute in goods.

questions.explanation: Both empires used local leaders. The Incas also moved some communities and spread a shared language alongside local ones. The Mexica relied more on tribute collected through existing local rulers.

questions.stem: Ibn Battuta's account best supports which claim about the Mali Empire?

options.A: Its rulers had rejected Islam in favor of traditional religions.
options.B: Its rulers combined Islamic practices with older West African traditions.
options.C: Its government was run by a council of Arab merchants from North Africa.
options.D: Its rulers had given up older court customs after converting to Islam.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Ibn Battuta describes crowded mosques and children learning the Quran by heart.
rationales.B: Correct. Mali's people filled the mosques and memorized the Quran. The court also kept older customs, like the poets' ceremony, which came from "prior to the introduction of Islam."
rationales.C: Incorrect. The passage shows the sultan (the mansa) holding court with his musicians, poets, and armed guards. It does not mention any council of Arab merchants.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Ibn Battuta says the poets' custom came from before Islam "and that they have kept it up."

questions.explanation: Mali's kings were Muslim, which linked them to North Africa and the Middle East. They also kept older customs, like praise poetry. These customs built their power at home.

questions.stem: Ibn Battuta's criticisms in the last paragraph most likely reflect

options.A: his wish to stop Mali's ruler from selling gold to Europeans
options.B: his belief that the people of West Africa had not yet heard of Islam
options.C: his view, as a scholar from Morocco, of how proper Muslims should behave
options.D: his effort to win a high government position from the ruler of Mali

rationales.A: Incorrect. The passage does not mention trade with Europe.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Ibn Battuta praises Mali's crowded mosques and Quran lessons, so he knew its people were Muslims.
rationales.C: Correct. Ibn Battuta was trained in Islamic law. He judged women's dress and the dust ceremony by the rules he knew from Morocco.
rationales.D: Incorrect. He is describing customs he observed; nothing suggests he is seeking a job from the mansa.

questions.explanation: Ibn Battuta admired Mali's justice and its faithful prayer. But he disliked customs that did not fit his idea of Muslim behavior. His criticisms show his own point of view.

questions.stem: The wealth of Mali's court, shown by the gold described in the passage, came mainly from

options.A: tribute paid to Mali by the Mamluk sultans of Egypt
options.B: control of trade across the Sahara in gold and salt
options.C: taxes on spices shipped from India to the Swahili coast
options.D: selling horses raised in West Africa to North African buyers

rationales.A: Incorrect. Mansa Musa passed through Mamluk Egypt on his way to Mecca, but Egypt did not pay tribute to Mali.
rationales.B: Correct. Mali controlled gold fields and the trade routes across the Sahara. Gold went north; salt, horses, and cloth came south.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Swahili coast is in East Africa, far from Mali. That trade made cities like Kilwa rich.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Horses went the other way. Traders brought them south across the Sahara to sell in West Africa.

questions.explanation: Mali grew rich by taxing trade across the Sahara. Gold went north, and salt came south. The same trade brought Muslim scholars like Ibn Battuta.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a similarity between the two sources?

options.A: Both protect nobles' powers against a central ruler.
options.B: Both give the pope the power to choose kings and emperors.
options.C: Both free serfs and give peasants the right to own land.
options.D: Both create a standing army paid for by royal taxes.

rationales.A: Correct. Magna Carta lets 25 barons force the king to keep his promises. The Golden Bull lets the prince electors choose the emperor and keep mines and tolls.
rationales.B: Incorrect. In Source 2 the electors, not the pope, choose the king, and Source 1 does not mention the pope.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Neither source frees serfs. Magna Carta protects "freemen."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Neither source creates a royal army; both limit the ruler's power.

questions.explanation: In England and in the Holy Roman Empire, powerful nobles got their rights written down. These rules kept rulers from gaining too much power.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the political arrangements in the two sources?

options.A: English barons chose each new king; the electors served as advisers to the emperor.
options.B: English barons controlled the royal mines; the electors controlled the Church courts.
options.C: English barons relied on the pope to limit the king; the electors approved the emperor's taxes.
options.D: English barons could enforce the charter against the king; the electors chose the ruler.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Magna Carta does not let the barons choose the king. In Source 2, the electors choose the ruler; they are not just his advisers.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Golden Bull, not Magna Carta, gives rights to mines, and it gives them to the electors. Neither excerpt says the electors controlled Church courts.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Neither excerpt relies on the pope. Magna Carta, not the Golden Bull, requires consent for certain payments.
rationales.D: Correct. Clause 61 lets 25 barons force King John to keep his promises. The Golden Bull names the prince electors who choose the king of the Romans, the future emperor.

questions.explanation: Both documents limited rulers, but in different ways. English barons could force the king to keep the charter. The German electors chose the ruler himself.

questions.stem: The principle stated in clause 12 of Source 1 is most closely connected to which later development in England?

options.A: Parliament's growing role in approving taxes
options.B: The king's growing power to tax without the nobles' consent
options.C: The end of serfdom in England in the 1200s
options.D: The pope's power to approve or reject English taxes

rationales.A: Correct. Clause 12 says the king needs "common counsel" to raise certain taxes. Over time, kings called Parliaments to give that agreement, and Parliament's power grew.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Clause 12 limited the king's power to tax. Over time, kings had to ask for consent more often, not less.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Clause 12 is about taxes on the barons and the realm, not serfs. Serfdom lasted in England long after 1215.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Clause 12 says taxes need the "common counsel" of the realm, not the pope's approval.

questions.explanation: Clause 12 said the king needed the "common counsel" of the realm before raising scutage or certain aids. This clause was left out when Magna Carta was reissued in 1216, but the idea lived on. Later kings called Parliaments to agree to new taxes, and Parliament grew stronger.

questions.stem: The scene in the painting best illustrates which feature of European society from c. 1200 to c. 1450?

options.A: Most people were peasants who farmed land on a lord's estate.
options.B: Most people lived in large cities and worked for merchant guilds.
options.C: Most peasants owned their own farms and did not work for a lord.
options.D: Farm work was done mainly by paid laborers hired by city merchants.

rationales.A: Correct. Peasants plow, prune vines, and tend sheep in the fields below a lord's castle. Europe was mostly a farming society, and much land was organized into manors.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The painting shows country fields, and most Europeans lived in the countryside, not in cities.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Most peasants farmed land that belonged to a lord, and they owed him work, fees, or crops.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Most farm workers were peasants tied to a lord's land, not workers hired by merchants.

questions.explanation: Most Europeans in this period were peasants. Their work produced food and wealth on estates controlled by nobles. Some peasants were serfs; others had more rights.

questions.stem: The painting was most likely intended to

options.A: protest the harsh treatment of peasants by French nobles
options.B: teach peasants new farming methods in their own language
options.C: persuade knights to join a crusade
options.D: honor its rich owner by showing his orderly lands

rationales.A: Incorrect. The peasants work calmly. The painting does not show suffering or protest.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The book was a costly prayer book made for a duke's private use. Its pictures were not lessons for farmers.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The painting shows farm work, not war or a crusade.
rationales.D: Correct. The book was a costly prayer book made for the Duke of Berry, a royal prince. Its calendar page shows his castle above calm, busy fields, a flattering picture of his lands.

questions.explanation: This page comes from the calendar of a costly prayer book made for the duke. It links the month of March with seasonal farm work and shows his lands as calm and orderly. Real peasant life was often harder.

questions.stem: Which development from c. 1200 to c. 1450 most strongly challenged the kind of local power represented by the castle?

options.A: The granting of country estates to knights in return for military service
options.B: The growth of the dues that peasants owed to the owners of estates
options.C: The inheritance of noble titles and family estates from father to son
options.D: Kings' growing use of royal courts and taxes to extend their power

rationales.A: Incorrect. Granting estates to knights created more local lords. It built up local power instead of challenging it.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Higher dues from peasants made estate owners richer and stronger, not weaker.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Passing titles and lands down within noble families helped local power last. It did not challenge it.
rationales.D: Correct. In England and France, kings built up royal courts and collected more taxes in this period. Over time, royal government reached into lands that lords had once run on their own.

questions.explanation: Castles were homes and forts for lords who ruled their own areas. In this period, some kings expanded royal courts and collected more taxes. In France, kings began collecting regular taxes during the Hundred Years' War. These changes reached into areas where nobles had held local power.
